title: "Finding Spatial Clusters with DBSCAN"
date: 2026-09-09
categories: [tool, geoml, bilingual]
description: "An interactive lab with Python, R and MapLibre — run DBSCAN on a set of points, see how a distance in meters requires picking a real coordinate system first, and why the two languages label the exact same groups with different numbers."
---

Some questions aren't "is this one point inside that polygon" — they're
"which of these points belong together, and which don't belong
anywhere." DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications
with Noise) answers that by density: a point belongs to a cluster if
enough other points sit close enough to it — no need to decide the
number of clusters in advance, and no need to force every point into
a group. A point too far from everything else stays *noise*, not a
cluster of one.

Want to try it on your own file instead of reading through the code?
Use the [standalone tool](/tools/spatial-clustering-explorer.html) —
same engine, less prose.

## 1. Why the coordinate system matters here

DBSCAN takes one distance, ε (`eps`): how close two points need to be
to count as neighbors. For that distance to mean anything, it has to
be in real units — meters — not degrees of longitude/latitude, where
the same number of degrees covers very different real distances
depending on where on Earth you are. Both languages below pick a
working UTM zone from the data's own bounding-box center and
reproject into it first — same reasoning, same formula, as this
site's [Viewshed](raster-viewshed.qmd) tool: a reasonable default for
one local dataset, not a universally correct choice for points
spanning multiple UTM zones or very large areas.

## 2. Same spatial question, two languages

Fourteen points, laid out on purpose: two tight groups of six, and two
points far from everything — including each other. Fixed coordinates,
not uploaded or randomly generated: the point here is the algorithm
and how the two languages report it, not file handling (the
[standalone tool](/tools/spatial-clustering-explorer.html) covers
uploading a real file).

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #spatial-clustering-py}
#| package: scikit-learn, pyproj
import numpy as np
from pyproj import Transformer
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

POINTS = [
    [12.4500, 41.9000], [12.4503, 41.9002], [12.4498, 41.8998],
    [12.4501, 41.9001], [12.4499, 41.8999], [12.4502, 41.9003],
    [12.4700, 41.9050], [12.4703, 41.9052], [12.4698, 41.9048],
    [12.4701, 41.9051], [12.4699, 41.9049], [12.4702, 41.9053],
    [12.4300, 41.8800],
    [12.5000, 41.9300]
]

lons = np.array([p[0] for p in POINTS])
lats = np.array([p[1] for p in POINTS])

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
center_lon = (lons.min() + lons.max()) / 2
center_lat = (lats.min() + lats.max()) / 2
utm_zone = int((center_lon + 180) // 6) + 1
calc_epsg = 32600 + utm_zone if center_lat >= 0 else 32700 + utm_zone

transformer = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326", f"EPSG:{calc_epsg}", always_xy=True)
xs, ys = transformer.transform(lons, lats)
coords = np.column_stack([xs, ys])

# scikit-learn's own convention: noise is -1, real clusters start at 0.
labels = DBSCAN(eps=100, min_samples=4).fit(coords).labels_

{
    "calculationCrs": f"EPSG:{calc_epsg}",
    "labels": [int(l) for l in labels],
    "uniqueLabels": sorted(int(l) for l in set(labels)),
    "noiseCount": int((labels == -1).sum())
}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #spatial-clustering-r}
#| package: dbscan, sf, jsonlite
library(dbscan)
library(sf)

points <- rbind(
  c(12.4500, 41.9000), c(12.4503, 41.9002), c(12.4498, 41.8998),
  c(12.4501, 41.9001), c(12.4499, 41.8999), c(12.4502, 41.9003),
  c(12.4700, 41.9050), c(12.4703, 41.9052), c(12.4698, 41.9048),
  c(12.4701, 41.9051), c(12.4699, 41.9049), c(12.4702, 41.9053),
  c(12.4300, 41.8800),
  c(12.5000, 41.9300)
)

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
center_lon <- (min(points[, 1]) + max(points[, 1])) / 2
center_lat <- (min(points[, 2]) + max(points[, 2])) / 2
utm_zone <- floor((center_lon + 180) / 6) + 1
calc_epsg <- if (center_lat >= 0) 32600 + utm_zone else 32700 + utm_zone

pts_sf <- st_as_sf(data.frame(lon = points[, 1], lat = points[, 2]), coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
coords_calc <- st_coordinates(st_transform(pts_sf, calc_epsg))

# dbscan's own convention: noise is 0, real clusters start at 1 -- a
# real point of divergence from scikit-learn, not a formatting detail.
# See section 3 below.
res <- dbscan(coords_calc, eps = 100, minPts = 4)

result <- list(
  calculationCrs = jsonlite::unbox(paste0("EPSG:", calc_epsg)),
  labels = as.integer(res$cluster),
  uniqueLabels = sort(unique(as.integer(res$cluster))),
  noiseCount = jsonlite::unbox(as.integer(sum(res$cluster == 0)))
)
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

:::

}

## 3. A label is not a name

Both cards above found the same thing: two groups of six, and two
noise points. But the *numbers* don't match — and that's not a bug in
either language.

Two separate reasons, easy to conflate:

- **DBSCAN's own cluster numbering is arbitrary.** Nothing about
  "cluster 0" or "cluster 1" is meaningful on its own — it's just the
  order the algorithm happened to visit points in. Run the same
  algorithm again with the points in a different order (or on a
  different implementation entirely) and the *groupings* can come out
  identical while the *numbers* attached to them differ.
- **scikit-learn and `dbscan` also disagree on noise, specifically.**
  This one isn't arbitrary — it's a real, documented difference
  between the two libraries: scikit-learn labels noise `-1` and starts
  real clusters at `0`; R's `dbscan` package labels noise `0` and
  starts real clusters at `1`. Every non-noise label is shifted by
  exactly one.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
labelTable = {
  const wrap = document.createElement("div");
  if (!pySummary || !rSummary) {
    wrap.textContent = "Run both cells above to compare.";
    return wrap;
  }
  const table = document.createElement("table");
  table.className = "webgeods-stat-grid";
  table.style.display = "table";
  table.style.width = "100%";

  const headRow = document.createElement("tr");
  ["Point #", "Python label", "R label"].forEach((h) => {
    const th = document.createElement("th");
    th.className = "webgeods-stat-label";
    th.textContent = h;
    headRow.appendChild(th);
  });
  table.appendChild(headRow);

  pySummary.labels.forEach((pyLabel, i) => {
    const tr = document.createElement("tr");
    [String(i + 1), String(pyLabel), String(rSummary.labels[i])].forEach((text) => {
      const td = document.createElement("td");
      td.className = "webgeods-stat-value";
      td.textContent = text;
      tr.appendChild(td);
    });
    table.appendChild(tr);
  });

  wrap.appendChild(table);
  return wrap;
}
```

${labelTable}

Read down the table: every point Python calls `0`, R calls `1`; every
point Python calls `1`, R calls `2`; every point Python calls `-1`
(noise), R calls `0`. The *partition* — which points end up
together — is identical. The *labels* attached to it aren't, and
never had to be.

::: {.callout-note}
This is why comparing two clustering results — across languages, or
across two runs of the same algorithm — should compare **who's grouped
with whom**, never raw label equality. In practice: pick any two
points, and ask "does language A say they're in the same group, and
does language B agree?" — repeat for every pair, and you're comparing
partitions, not numbers that were never meant to match.
:::
